title: Collective sliding relaxor ferroelectricity across thousand-layer van der Waals superstructures
authors: Nianze Shang, Cuiju Yu, Yucai Lin, Juan C. Arias-Muñoz, Jiajie Qi, Quanlin Guo, MD Gius Uddin, Youqiang Huang, Tuomas Pajunpää, Christopher P. Edwards, Rodolfo E. Canet-Albiach, Faisal Ahmed, Andreas C. Liapis, Yaoqiang Zhou, Zhibin Zhang, Hao Hong, Qing Dai, Andrea Alù, José L. Lado, Kaihui Liu, Zhipei Sun
abstract: Relaxor ferroelectrics are among the most important electromechanical materials owing to their exceptionally large electrostrictive responses. However, conventional relaxor behavior is generally associated with chemical complexity and structural disorder, where local compositional fluctuations generate polar nanoregions, making the microscopic origin of this behavior difficult to control and engineer. Here we report sliding relaxor ferroelectricity (S-RFE), a previously unknown relaxor state in which engineered stacking-phase heterogeneity enables cooperative interlayer sliding to generate collective relaxor behavior. Through stacking-phase engineering in rhombohedral boron nitride, we create sliding domains that act as structural analogues of polar nanoregions and cooperatively align under an electric field through interlayer sliding. This collective state produces reversible electromechanical deformation of up to approximately $-1.6\%$ with negligible hysteresis in approximately 300-nm-thick crystals, corresponding to approximately 1000 atomic layers. The resulting electrostriction coefficient ($Q_{33}$ of approximately $1200\,\mathrm{m}^{4}\mathrm{C}^{-2}$) exceeds those of most crystalline electrostrictors by orders of magnitude. Unlike conventional relaxors, whose electromechanical response is often suppressed by dipolar freezing at low temperatures, S-RFE remains active down to 1.6 K and maintains giant electromechanical functionality. Our results establish sliding relaxor ferroelectricity as a new route to relaxor behavior and reveal how atomic-scale interlayer motion can be amplified into collective mesoscale functionality across approximately one thousand layers, providing a materials-by-design platform for electromechanical, photonic, and quantum technologies based on van der Waals materials.
summary: This work introduces Sliding Relaxor Ferroelectricity (S-RFE) in van der Waals boron nitride, showing that structural design, rather than chemical disorder, can yield giant ferroelectric responses. By engineering coexisting stacking phases, the material exhibits collective interlayer sliding that results in massive electrostriction. This establishes a new, highly controllable platform for advanced electromechanical and photonic devices.
main_problem: To establish a new, structurally engineered route to achieve relaxor ferroelectricity (S-RFE) that bypasses the need for chemical disorder.
main_result: The authors demonstrate that collective interlayer sliding in engineered van der Waals superstructures can generate giant electromechanical responses, achieving electrostriction coefficients orders of magnitude larger than conventional materials.
method: The study combines experimental characterization (TEM, PFM, optical spectroscopy) with theoretical modeling (DFT calculations) to map the phase transitions and electromechanical coupling.
model_or_system: The system is rhombohedral boron nitride (rBN) grown as a van der Waals superlattice, which exhibits engineered stacking-phase heterogeneity (coexisting ABC and CBA domains). The ferroelectric behavior arises from the cooperative sliding between these distinct stacking phases under an applied electric field.
key_observables: Reversible electromechanical deformation ($\sim -1.6\%$), electrostriction coefficient ($Q_{33} \sim 1200 	ext{ m}^4	ext{C}^{-2}$), and spectral shifts in Fabry-Pérot cavities.
important_parameters: Thickness scale ($\sim 1000$ atomic layers), operating temperature range (down to $1.6 	ext{ K}$), and applied electric field strength.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the observed spectral shift is directly proportional to the thickness change induced by the polarization switching, and that the electrostriction coefficient can be derived from a quadratic fit to the voltage dependence.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the mechanism contrasting conventional RFE with S-RFE, show TEM confirmation of coexisting stacking phases, and demonstrate the giant electrostriction via spectral shifts in F-P cavities across varying temperatures.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first defining the problem (disorder-based RFE), introducing the S-RFE concept based on structural engineering in rBN, providing multi-modal evidence (TEM, PFM, DFT) for the sliding mechanism, and finally quantifying the giant electromechanical response using optical spectroscopy.
why_interesting: While the primary focus is condensed matter electro-optics, the concept of emergent collective behavior from engineered atomic-scale interfaces (interlayer sliding) is analogous to studying collective excitations or phase transitions in artificial quantum materials or engineered quantum simulators.
